name: Hatomugi (job's tears) extract

card.summary: A grain extract from job's tears (Coix lacryma-jobi) that Japanese lotions and skin conditioners use to hydrate and smooth the skin.
card.note: Cosmetic ingredient; published skin studies are limited.

quick.overview:
Hatomugi is the Japanese name for job's tears, a tall grass grown for its grain. Extract from the seed is a long-standing ingredient in Japanese skin lotions and conditioners, where it is marketed to leave skin smooth, hydrated and clearer-looking.
The grain is also eaten and used in traditional Asian medicine. Published laboratory work has examined hatomugi extracts in cultured cells, and there is little published human clinical research on the skin lotion use.
quick.how: Hatomugi appears as a watery lotion or skin conditioner that is patted on or applied with a cotton pad after cleansing, often before a moisturizer, and as an ingredient in other products. Users typically describe using it daily over weeks.
quick.risks: As a cosmetic extract it is generally well tolerated, but any plant extract can cause reactions in sensitive skin. A 1985 Japanese survey of food contaminants found mycotoxins in job's-tears grain sold as a health food, relevant to ingesting grain rather than to topical products.

lead: Hatomugi is the Japanese name for job's tears (Coix lacryma-jobi), a tropical grass whose grain is eaten as a cereal and brewed as tea, and is used in traditional Chinese and folk medicine.[1] An extract of the seed is used in skin lotions, which in Japan have become a familiar everyday product.

People use hatomugi products to keep skin hydrated and smooth-looking, so it belongs to the basic-skin-care end of appearance routines. Marketing and user reviews describe soothing and clarifying effects, but these are claims from brands and users.

A laboratory study of Hatomugi-derived oat-type extracts (labelled SPH) looked at lipid-droplet formation in mouse preadipocytes and protection of human keratinocytes against hydrogen peroxide, work that concerns cells rather than lotions on skin.[2]

chain: Hatomugi extract applied as a lotion
Hydrates the surface of the skin
angle.text: It is applied after cleansing as a hydrating lotion to leave skin looking smoother. The benefit described is a cosmetic one based on brand and user reports.

paras: Job's tears is a tall tropical grass native to Southeast Asia. The grain is cooked as a cereal, milled into flour and brewed into drinks such as Japanese hatomugi tea, and the polished kernel, known in Chinese as yiyi ren, is used in Chinese cooking and medicine.[1] The seed contains roughly 65 percent carbohydrate, 14 percent protein and 5 percent fat.[1]
In skin products, hatomugi extract is typically an ingredient in watery lotions applied after cleansing. Skin-care discussion groups it with other grain and plant extracts used for hydration.

A 1985 survey of food products in Japan reported high-level contamination of job's-tears health-food samples with the mycotoxins nivalenol and zearalenone.[3] The survey concerned food products, not cosmetics.

No human skin trials of hatomugi lotions have been found. Laboratory work on Hatomugi-derived extracts reported reduced lipid-droplet formation in mouse preadipocytes and some protection of human keratinocytes from hydrogen-peroxide cell death.[2]
